catalog_quote: Representative word lists were chosen from each language group as follows: Uhak (Perai); Ilputih(b) (Aputai); Ilwaki (Talur); Ilway (Tugun); Ilmaumau (Ili'uun). [Editor's note: Since writing this paper the author has spent ten months living in the Tugun speaking area doing research on that language. He writes, "I know that there are no monosyllabic words in Tugun, and I suspect the same is true for the others. When I took the word lists, I was not in tune to vowel length, and didn't record it. Only after spending more time in the Tugun language did I analyse it as a sequence of like vowels." Since this is also true for languages in the wider region, monosyllabic lexical words (i.e. non-functors) in the following lists should be reinterpreted as having sequences of like vowels. E.g. /un/ should be assumed to be /uun/, /ron/ to be /roon/, and so forth. Word stress remains penultimate. --CEG] ... Symbols ... ' Stress in Wetar languages is generally penultimate. It is marked with an apostrophe preceding the stressed syllable where different.

new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (246 pp., ANU open repository, CC BY-SA). p. 129 = printed p. 119 'The languages of Wetar', Appendix B 'Comparative word lists', Symbols key: 'Stress in Wetar languages is generally penultimate. It is marked with an apostrophe preceding the stressed syllable where different.' is there verbatim. Editor's note on the same page ends '.. Word stress remains penultimate. --CEG' verbatim; the only differences are text-layer artefacts (the slashes in /un/, /uun/, /ron/, /roon/ render as 'lun!', 'luun!', 'Iron!', 'lroon!' and the initials as '--CEQ'); the compiler ellipsis and normalisation are fair. Surrounding section: Appendix B reproduces lists for Uhak (Perai), Ilputih(b) (Aputai), Ilwa…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In the Wetar survey languages, including Talur/Ilwaki (the Wetar dialect of Galoli), word stress falls on the penultimate syllable; deviations would be marked with an apostrophe in the word lists, and no Talur form in the lists carries one. Editor adds that after reinterpreting apparent monosyllables as like-vowel sequences (/uun/, /roon/) stress remains penultimate.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Talur/Galoli. For Tugun (a different Wetar language) the aspectual clitics -e and -me shift stress to the ultimate syllable of the root (p. 115-116).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in a survey word-list key; forms are citation forms elicited in a lexicostatistical survey. Covers Wetar languages as a group, not mainland Galoli specifically.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is Hinton's group-level remark for the Wetar survey languages; it applies to Galoli only through the Talur (Ilwaki) dialect spoken in three villages of south Wetar (Glottolog talu1239, dialect of galo1243; Grimes & Edwards 2026 treat Talur as a dialect of Galolen and Hinton 2000 reports 86% lexical similarity with Capell's Galoli). Mainland Galoli (Manatuto, Laclo, Laleia) has no accessible stress statement; the mainland sketches (Hull 2003, Sadnyana et al. 1994, da Silva 1900) were not obtainable. Dadu'a, sometimes listed as a Galoli dialect, is a transplanted Atauro/Wetarese variety per Wikipedia and Grimes & Edwards 2026.

sources.note: Symbol key to the survey word lists (which include Ilwaki = Talur, the Wetar dialect of Galoli), p. 119: 'Stress in Wetar languages is generally penultimate. It is marked with an apostrophe preceding the stressed syllable where different.'; editor's note (C. Grimes) same page: 'Word stress remains penultimate.' No Talur form in the lists (pp. 120-129) carries a stress mark. Tugun-specific rule p. 115-116: penultimate, aspectual clitics -e/-me shift it to the ultimate of the root.

sources.note: Galolen is treated in section 4.5 Wetar-Atauro (pp. 194-201) for subgrouping only; no Galolen-specific stress statement. General remark p. 115: 'While penultimate stress is the normal rule for Wallacean languages, words with penultimate schwa can have stress on other syllables.' Appendix A p. 736 lists the Galolen data sources: Cristo Rei & Grimes 2011 (Disionariu Galolen), Cristo Rei & Donohue 2012 (unpublished dictionary), Dawson 2014 (PARADISEC VD1); Talur: Hinton 2000.
